key_concept: An octahedral complex is chiral (optically active) only if it has no plane or centre of symmetry; complexes of type $[M(AA)_3]$ and cis-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ are chiral, while trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ is not.
steps: Oxalate, $ox^{2-}$ ($C_2O_4^{2-}$), is a symmetrical bidentate ligand (AA type).

Statement I: $[Fe(ox)_3]^{3-}$ is of the type $[M(AA)_3]$. The three chelate rings wrap around the metal like a propeller, giving $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ forms. These are non-superimposable mirror images.
$[M(AA)_3]$ has no plane of symmetry and no centre of symmetry, so it is chiral. Statement I is correct.
Statement II: trans-$[Cr(H_2O)_2(ox)_2]^-$ is of the type trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$. The two $H_2O$ ligands sit on the axis, and both oxalate rings lie in the equatorial plane.
That equatorial plane is a mirror plane, and the complex also has a centre of symmetry. So its mirror image is superimposable and the complex is achiral. Statement II is incorrect.
(Only the cis isomer of $[Cr(H_2O)_2(ox)_2]^-$ is optically active.)
final_answer: Option (3): Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
why_not_others: Options (1) and (4) would require the trans isomer to be chiral, but its equatorial mirror plane rules this out. Option (2) wrongly denies the well-known $\Delta/\Lambda$ optical isomerism of $[M(AA)_3]$ complexes.
common_trap: Students often assume any complex containing chelating ligands is optically active, forgetting that the trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ arrangement has a plane of symmetry.
time_saving_tip: Memorise the rule: $[M(AA)_3]$ and cis-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ are chiral; trans-$[M(AA)_2B_2]$ is never chiral.
